title: Brachial Plexus Anatomy: C5–T1 Roots, Trunks & Branches
description: Learn brachial plexus anatomy from spinal roots C5–T1 through trunks, divisions, and cords to musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, and ulnar nerves.
h1: Brachial Plexus Anatomy (C5–T1): Roots, Trunks, Cords and Arm Nerves
blurb: How spinal nerve roots C5–T1 braid into trunks, divisions, and cords to form the musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median, and ulnar nerves of the upper limb.
lead: Crossing from the lateral neck through the axilla into the upper limb, the brachial plexus braids five spinal nerve roots into the motor and sensory cables of the arm and hand. In this illustrated guide to brachial plexus nerve anatomy, we examine 20 documented structures—including c5–t1 ventral rami, interscalene passage, upper trunk, middle trunk—linking regional topography, tissue architecture, physiological mechanisms, and clinical reasoning.
overview: Crossing from the lateral neck through the axilla into the upper limb, the brachial plexus braids five spinal nerve roots into the motor and sensory cables of the arm and hand. The brachial plexus usually arises from ventral rami C5–T1. C5–6 form upper trunk, C7 middle trunk and C8–T1 lower trunk. Each trunk divides anteriorly and posteriorly; anterior divisions of upper/middle form lateral cord, lower forms medial cord, all posterior divisions form posterior cord. Cords are named relative to the axillary artery. Musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves reach the limb; several important scapular and pectoral branches leave the plexus before these endpoints. Within the human body, the brachial plexus · arm nerves (Plexus brachialis) is situated in c5–T1 ventral rami between scalene muscles → behind clavicle → axilla and upper limb, receives arterial perfusion via cords surround axillary artery; regional supply from subclavian/axillary branches, and is innervated by ventral rami C5–T1, with frequent prefixed/postfixed variation.

The c5–T1 ventral rami (Rami anteriores C5–T1) is five spinal nerve ventral rami build the typical plexus; not the intrathecal dorsal/ventral rootlets. Physiologically, the c5–T1 ventral rami provide segmental motor and sensory fibers to upper limb. Structurally, the interscalene passage (Spatium interscalenum) comprises roots and trunks pass between anterior and middle scalene muscles. Physiologically, the interscalene passage governs conveys plexus out of neck. Structurally, the upper trunk (Truncus superior) comprises formed by union of C5 and C6 ventral rami. Physiologically, the upper trunk governs redistributes upper-root fibers into divisions. Structurally, the middle trunk (Truncus medius) comprises continuation of C7 ventral ramus. Physiologically, the middle trunk feeds anterior and posterior divisions. Structurally, the lower trunk (Truncus inferior) comprises formed by C8 and T1 ventral rami. Physiologically, the lower trunk carries lower-root fibers toward hand pathways. The anterior divisions (Divisiones anteriores) are one anterior division from each trunk, usually destined for limb flexor compartments. Physiologically, the anterior divisions governs create lateral and medial cords.

Clinically, regarding the c5–T1 ventral rami, anatomy can be prefixed C4–C8 or postfixed C6–T2. From a diagnostic standpoint, in the interscalene passage, site of interscalene regional anesthesia. In clinical pathology involving the upper trunk, upper-trunk traction can weaken shoulder abduction and elbow flexion. Medical evaluation of the middle trunk also notes that c7 contribution enters multiple terminal nerves.

questions.question: What are the five major terminal branches of the brachial plexus?
questions.answer: Musculocutaneous, axillary, radial, median and ulnar nerves are the five commonly taught terminal branches. Structurally, the medial cord (Fasciculus medialis) comprises continuation of lower trunk anterior division, medial to axillary artery. Physiologically, the medial cord gives ulnar and medial root of median nerve.
